lead: This unit builds the smallest computing machine there is, the finite automaton, and ties it to the sets of strings it accepts. You will learn to design deterministic and nondeterministic machines, to convert one into the other, and to shrink a machine to its smallest form. After it you can write a machine for a given language and argue that two machines accept exactly the same strings.
about: The unit starts with the raw material: alphabets, strings and languages (1.1). Chapter 1.2 defines the deterministic finite automaton, a machine with one state and exactly one move per symbol, and 1.3 gives the two notations, diagram and table, plus the extended transition function that turns a machine into a language. Chapters 1.4 and 1.5 loosen the rules: many moves at once, then moves that read no input. Chapter 1.6 shows the loosening costs nothing by building a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states. Chapter 1.7 shrinks a DFA to its smallest form, 1.8 adds printed output to states and transitions, and 1.9, taught in only a few universities, lets the read head move both ways.

chapters.idea: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of them, and a language is simply a set of strings.
chapters.depth: Define alphabet Σ (finite, non-empty), symbol, string (some syllabi say word), the empty string ε, length |w|, and the sets Σ* (all finite strings including ε) and Σ⁺ = Σ* − {ε}. Define concatenation, powers wⁿ, reverse wᴿ, prefix, suffix, substring. Define a language as any subset of Σ*. Cover the operations on languages: union, intersection, complement relative to Σ*, difference, concatenation L₁L₂, powers Lⁿ, Kleene star L*, Kleene plus L⁺. Show ∅* = {ε}. State the set membership problem: given a string w and a language L, decide whether w ∈ L — this is the question the whole unit answers. Note that Σ* is infinite but countable, while the set of all languages over Σ is uncountable, so most languages have no machine at all.

figure.aria: An outer box labelled sigma-star holds four short strings, and an inner box labelled L holds the four strings of length two.
figure.caption: L = {00, 01, 10, 11} is a subset of Σ*, so it is a language over {0, 1}.

chapters.example: Σ = {0, 1} and L = {w ∈ Σ* : |w| = 2} = {00, 01, 10, 11}. Find L², L* and the complement of L. Answer: L² is every string uv with u, v ∈ L, that is all 16 strings of length 4, and no two pairs give the same string. L* = {ε} ∪ L ∪ L² ∪ … is the set of all even-length strings, because any even length splits into blocks of 2 and an odd length never does. The complement of L is the set of all odd-length strings.
chapters.trap: ε is a string of length 0, {ε} is a one-element language and ∅ is the empty language: three different objects, and ∅* = {ε}. A second slip is mixing symbols with strings, so write the string 0 in quotes when it is an element of a language.
chapters.leave: Regular expressions and the algebraic laws of languages go to Unit 2; grammars go to Unit 3; the counting argument that most languages have no machine is only stated here.

chapters.idea: A DFA is a machine with finite memory: one state that holds everything about the past that can change the future, updated one symbol at a time.
chapters.depth: Give the formal definition as a 5-tuple M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): Q a finite non-empty set of states, Σ the input alphabet, δ: Q × Σ → Q a total function, q₀ ∈ Q the start state, F ⊆ Q the final (accepting) states. Explain every term. Stress determinism: exactly one next state for each state and symbol, no choice, no ε. Define the run on w = a₁a₂…aₙ and the language L(M) = {w ∈ Σ* : the run on w ends in a state of F}. Some syllabi list 'simplified notation' here — the short form where the diagram replaces the tuple. Teach design by 'remember the least you must': strings ending in ab, strings containing 01, number of a's divisible by 3, strings with no two consecutive 1s. Introduce the dead (trap) state.

figure.aria: Three circles A, B and C joined by labelled arrows; C is the only double circle and the arrow marked 1 sends C back to A.
figure.caption: State C is the only accepting state, so the machine accepts exactly the strings ending in 01.

chapters.example: Design a DFA over Σ = {0, 1} that accepts exactly the strings ending in 01, and test it on 1001 and 110. Answer: take Q = {A, B, C}, q₀ = A, F = {C}. Transitions: A on 0 goes to B, A on 1 stays at A, B on 0 stays at B, B on 1 goes to C, C on 0 goes to B, C on 1 goes to A. Read 1001: A, A, B, B, C — C is final, so 1001 is accepted. Read 110: A, A, A, B — B is not final, so 110 is rejected.
chapters.trap: A table with missing entries is not a DFA: δ must be total, so add a dead state rather than leaving a cell blank. Also remember the start state may itself be final, and a final state still needs all its outgoing moves.
chapters.leave: The recursion for δ̂ and the table layout go to 1.3; allowing many moves at once goes to 1.4; closure and decision properties go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The extended transition function δ̂ answers 'where do I end up after a whole string', and acceptance is defined with it.
chapters.depth: Describe the transition diagram conventions: circles for states, a short incoming arrow for q₀, a double circle for each state in F, directed edges labelled by symbols, separate parallel edges when two symbols cause the same move. Describe the transition table: one row per state, one column per symbol, entries are states. Define δ̂ (some books write δ*): δ̂(q, ε) = q and δ̂(q, wa) = δ(δ̂(q, w), a). Note the recursion peels the last symbol. State L(M) = {w ∈ Σ* : δ̂(q₀, w) ∈ F} and prove δ̂(q, xy) = δ̂(δ̂(q, x), y) by induction on |y|. Trace a string column by column.

figure.title: δ̂(A, 1001) step by step
figure.aria: A five-row table showing the state reached after each prefix of 1001 and whether that state is final.
figure.caption: The last row is the answer: δ̂(A, 1001) = C, a final state, so 1001 is accepted.

chapters.example: For the machine of 1.2 with states A, B, C, compute δ̂(A, 1001) and δ̂(A, 110) and decide acceptance. δ̂(A, 1001): δ̂(A, ε) = A; δ̂(A, 1) = δ(A, 1) = A; δ̂(A, 10) = δ(A, 0) = B; δ̂(A, 100) = δ(B, 0) = B; δ̂(A, 1001) = δ(B, 1) = C. C is final, so 1 001 is accepted. δ̂(A, 110): A, then A, then A, then δ(A, 0) = B, which is not final, so 110 is rejected.
chapters.trap: Keep δ and δ̂ apart: δ takes one symbol, δ̂ takes a whole string. The recursion removes the last symbol, not the first, so never read a string from the right.
chapters.leave: NFA tables whose entries are sets go to 1.4; turning these tables into regular expressions goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: An NFA may have zero, one or many moves on the same symbol, and it accepts when at least one run reaches a final state.
chapters.depth: Formal definition M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) with δ: Q × Σ → 2^Q, where 2^Q is the power set of Q, so the empty set is a legal entry. A run is a sequence of choices; w is accepted if some run ends in F. Draw the computation tree, one level per input symbol, and show that any root-to-leaf path that ends in F is enough. Explain nondeterminism as perfect guessing, which is a specification, not a program. Design examples: strings containing 01, strings ending in ab, the third symbol from the right is 1. Some syllabi write 'non-deterministic'. State, without proof here, that NFAs are no stronger than DFAs.

figure.aria: Four circles in a chain; the start state loops on 0 and 1 and also has an arrow to q1 on 1, and the chain ends in the double circle q3.
figure.caption: On a 1 the machine may stay in q0 or jump to q1; that jump is the guess that the third symbol from the right has just been read.

chapters.example: Build an NFA over {0, 1} for L = {w : the third symbol from the right is 1} and trace the set of states on input 0110. Answer: Q = {q0, q1, q2, q3}, q₀ = q0, F = {q3}; δ(q0, 0) = {q0}, δ(q0, 1) = {q0, q1}, δ(q1, 0) = δ(q1, 1) = {q2}, δ(q2, 0) = δ(q2, 1) = {q3}, δ(q3, ·) = ∅. Trace: {q0} on 0 gives {q0}; on 1 gives {q0, q1}; on 1 gives {q0, q1, q2}; on 0 gives {q0, q2, q3}. q3 is in the last set, so 0110 is accepted, and indeed its third symbol from the right is 1.
chapters.trap: δ(q, a) is a set, so writing a single state in the table is wrong. Also, one failing run does not reject the string — only the absence of any accepting run does.
chapters.leave: ε-moves go to 1.5; the proof that NFAs are no stronger than DFAs goes to 1.6; the pumping lemma for non-regular languages goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: An ε-transition changes state without reading input, so before each symbol the machine may be in any state of the ε-closure of its current set.
chapters.depth: Definition: δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2^Q. Some syllabi call this 'finite automata with ε-moves'. Define the ε-closure ECLOSE(q) as the set of states reachable from q using ε-edges only, always including q itself. Extend it to sets. Define δ̂ with closures: δ̂(q, ε) = ECLOSE(q) and δ̂(q, wa) = ECLOSE(∪ δ(p, a)) over p in δ̂(q, w). Give the language of an ε-NFA. Show ε-elimination: build an NFA with no ε-edges using δ'(q, a) = δ̂(q, a), and make q final in the new machine whenever ECLOSE(q) contains an old final state. State that ε-NFAs accept exactly the regular languages.

figure.aria: Four circles in a row; dashed arrows marked epsilon link q0 to q1 and q2 to q3 without reading a symbol, and q3 is the double circle.
figure.caption: Dashed arrows consume no input, so the machine is already in q1 before the first symbol, and in q3 as soon as it reaches q2.

chapters.example: For the machine above, find all ε-closures, then δ̂(q0, ab). ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1}, ECLOSE(q1) = {q1}, ECLOSE(q2) = {q2, q3}, ECLOSE(q3) = {q3}. Start: δ̂(q0, ε) = {q0, q1}. On a: the a-moves from q0 and q1 are q0 and none, so ECLOSE({q0}) = {q0, q1}. On b: the b-moves from q0 and q1 are none and q2, so ECLOSE({q2}) = {q2, q3}. q3 is final, so ab is accepted. Eliminating ε gives δ'(q0, a) = {q0, q1}, δ'(q0, b) = {q2, q3}, δ'(q2, a) = {q3}.
chapters.trap: The closure of the start state must be taken before the first symbol, and if a final state has ε-edges then the states it reaches are final in effect. Closure is not symmetric: ECLOSE(q0) may contain q1 while ECLOSE(q1) does not contain q0.
chapters.leave: Turning an ε-NFA into a DFA goes to 1.6; regular expressions for the same language go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A DFA state can be a whole set of NFA states, so one deterministic run simulates all the NFA runs at once.
chapters.depth: Subset construction (also called the powerset construction). Given N = (Q_N, Σ, δ_N, q₀, F_N), build D = (Q_D, Σ, δ_D, q_D0, F_D) with Q_D = 2^{Q_N}, q_D0 = ECLOSE({q₀}), δ_D(S, a) = ECLOSE(∪ δ_N(p, a)) over p in S, and F_D = {S ⊆ Q_N : S ∩ F_N ≠ ∅}. Build only reachable subsets, not all 2^n. Prove by induction on |w| that δ̂_D({q₀}, w) = δ̂_N(q₀, w), hence L(D) = L(N). State the worst-case bound of 2^n states and that it is achievable. Make clear that equivalence means equal languages, not equal numbers of states. The full pipeline some syllabi ask for is: remove ε-edges, then subset construction.

figure.aria: A left-to-right flow from an NFA through epsilon-closures and reachable subsets to a DFA table and finally a minimal DFA.
figure.caption: The middle box is the whole idea: each reachable set of NFA states becomes one DFA state.

chapters.example: Convert this NFA over {a, b} to a DFA: δ(q0, a) = {q0, q1}, δ(q0, b) = {q0}, δ(q1, b) = {q2}, δ(q1, a) = ∅, δ(q2, ·) = ∅, F = {q2}. Start set {q0} = A. A on a gives {q0, q1} = B; A on b gives {q0} = A. B on a gives {q0, q1} = B; B on b gives {q0, q2} = C. C on a gives {q0, q1} = B; C on b gives {q0} = A. So Q_D = {A, B, C}, start A, F_D = {C}: a 3-state DFA that accepts exactly the strings ending in ab.
chapters.trap: A subset is final if it contains at least one final state, not if all its states are final. Forgetting to close each new subset under ε, or listing subsets that can never be reached, are the other common errors.
chapters.leave: Minimising the DFA you just built goes to 1.7; the Myhill-Nerode proof of minimality goes to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Two states are equivalent when no string tells them apart, and the table-filling algorithm finds every distinguishable pair in rounds.
chapters.depth: Define distinguishability: p and q are distinguishable if some w ∈ Σ* sends exactly one of δ̂(p, w), δ̂(q, w) into F; otherwise they are equivalent. Give the marking (table-filling) algorithm: delete unreachable states; write every unordered pair once, as a triangular table; mark each pair with one final and one non-final state; then repeat over all unmarked pairs (p, q) and all a ∈ Σ, marking (p, q) if (δ(p, a), δ(q, a)) is already marked; stop when a pass marks nothing. Merge the unmarked pairs, build the quotient DFA on the classes, and state that the result is the unique minimal DFA up to renaming of states. Mention the link to the Myhill-Nerode right-invariant equivalence. Some syllabi call this 'distinguishing one string from another'.

figure.title: Pairs marked at each pass
figure.aria: A table of state pairs grouped by the round in which they were marked; the last row is empty, so the algorithm has stopped.
figure.caption: The third pass marks nothing new, so the only unmarked pair left, (q0, q3), gives two states that merge.

chapters.example: Minimise this DFA over {a, b}: q0 on a, b goes to q1, q3; q1 goes to q2, q1; q2 goes to q0, q2; q3 goes to q1, q3; F = {q0, q3}. Pass 0 marks the mixed pairs (q0, q1), (q0, q2), (q1, q3), (q2, q3). Pass 1 checks (q0, q3): both go to q1 on a and to q3 on b, so it stays unmarked; pair (q1, q2) goes to (q2, q0) on a, and (q0, q2) is marked, so (q1, q2) is marked. Pass 2 marks nothing. Classes: {q0, q3}, {q1}, {q2} — a 3-state DFA counting a's modulo 3.
chapters.trap: Delete unreachable states first, or they survive as extra classes. Do not stop after one pass: run until a pass marks nothing new. And two states that are both final, or both non-final, can still be distinguishable.
chapters.leave: The full Myhill-Nerode theorem and its proof go to Unit 2; minimising a Moore machine goes to 1.8.

chapters.idea: A Moore machine prints on entering a state and a Mealy machine prints on taking a transition, and each can be converted into the other.
chapters.depth: Moore machine: (Q, Σ, Δ, δ, λ, q₀), where Δ is the output alphabet and λ: Q → Δ prints the output of the state; there is no set of final states. Mealy machine: same tuple with λ: Q × Σ → Δ, written on the edge as a / b. For an input of n symbols a Moore machine prints n + 1 symbols, because the start state prints first; a Mealy machine prints n. Conversion Moore to Mealy: λ'(q, a) = λ(δ(q, a)). Conversion Mealy to Moore: each new state is a pair (old state, output printed when that state was entered). Both are finite-state transducers, not acceptors, and both are equally powerful. Uses: sequence detector, vending machine, traffic-light controller, digital lock, the token scanner inside a compiler. Some syllabi list 'equivalence of Moore and Mealy machines'.

figure.aria: Three circles A, B and C, each carrying a printed output value, joined by arrows labelled 0 and 1.
figure.caption: This is the Moore form of a 01 detector: only state C prints 1, and it is entered exactly when the input has just finished 01.

chapters.example: Design a Mealy machine over {0, 1} that prints 1 whenever the last two bits read are 01, and convert it to Moore. Mealy: states S0 and S1; S0 on 0 goes to S1 printing 0, S0 on 1 stays at S0 printing 0, S1 on 0 stays at S1 printing 0, S1 on 1 goes to S0 printing 1. On input 0101 the output is 0101. Moore version: states A = (S0, 0), B = (S1, 0), C = (S0, 1) with outputs 0, 0, 1; A on 0 goes to B and on 1 to A, B on 0 to B and on 1 to C, C on 0 to B and on 1 to A. On the same input the Moore output is 00101 — the same sequence with one extra symbol in front.
chapters.trap: The Moore output is one symbol longer than the Mealy output for the same input, so do not compare them position by position. Also, a Mealy machine can have fewer states than the Moore machine that does the same job.
chapters.leave: These transducers appear as lexical analysers in the applications of Unit 2; machines that also print or write are Turing machines, in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A two-way finite automaton may move its read head left or right, yet it still accepts only regular languages.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic, so keep it short. Definition: a two-way FA is (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) with δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {⊢, ⊣}) → Q × {L, R}; the input sits on a tape with a left end marker ⊢ and a right end marker ⊣ so the head never falls off. The head may move left or right, and the machine accepts if it stops in a state of F. State the theorem without proof: deterministic and nondeterministic two-way FAs accept exactly the regular languages, the same class as ordinary DFAs. Give the reason in one line: the behaviour of the head on a prefix is fixed by a finite crossing sequence, so the language is regular. Note that the equivalent DFA can be exponentially larger.

figure.aria: Five circles; the head runs right along q1 until the end marker sends it one step left to q2, which accepts on a and falls into the dead state on b.
figure.caption: The arrow from q1 to q2 moves the head left: that single backward move is what an ordinary DFA cannot do.

chapters.example: Trace the two-way machine above on input aba and on input abb. On aba the tape is ⊢ a b a ⊣. Head on ⊢ in q0 moves right into q1. q1 reads a, moves right; reads b, moves right; reads a, moves right; reads ⊣ and moves left into q2. q2 reads the last symbol a and moves to qf, so aba is accepted. On abb the head again reaches q2 at the last symbol, but q2 on b goes to the dead state, so abb is rejected. The machine accepts exactly the strings that begin and end with a.
chapters.trap: Two-way movement does not add power, so claiming that a two-way FA accepts aⁿbⁿ is wrong. The head must also be stopped by end markers, and the transition function must be defined so the head can never move past them.
chapters.leave: The crossing-sequence proof and the exponential blow-up are beyond this unit; only the fact that the language is still regular is used later.
